raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old Italian man, who had been living in Nigeria because of his job since two years, was urgently repatriated following diagnosis of acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Fourteen days after anti-malarial treatment started, with quick resolution of fever, he suddenly complained of acute left flank pain.
At emergency department (ED) admission, his vital parameters appeared stable. Physical examination revealed tender left hemiabdomen without frank peritonism. Laboratory tests disclosed severe anemia (hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL), moderate leukocytosis, markedly elevated C-Reactive Protein (232 mg/L), plasma D-Dimer (2188 ug/L), lactic dehydrogenase (654 IU/L) and creatine kinase (1255 IU/L); platelet count and coagulation assays were within normal limits. Rapid blood assay tested positive for P. falciparum antigen, with negative blood cultures for bacteria and parasites.
Prompt investigation with multi-detector CT [Figure 1] allowed confident diagnosis of diffuse, moderately hyperdense peritoneal effusion consistent with hemoperitoneum and splenomegaly with hyperdense, stratified subcapsular and perisplenic clotted hematoma. Bilateral pleural effusion and lung base atelectasis were also present.
Urgent laparotomic surgery confirmed abundant hemorrhagic peritoneal effusion without detectable active bleeding. Splenomegaly with multiple blood clots was resected. Pathology specimen reported 850-g enlarged spleen measuring 17x14x8 cm after fixation, with large capsular interruption and underlying hematoma. Histologically, diffuse parenchymal hemorrhage and markedly hypertrophic red pulp were observed, without follicular structure abnormalities nor signs of malignancy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with sudden-onset acute left flank pain 14 days after starting treatment for a severe febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 42-year-old male who had resided in Nigeria for two years was urgently repatriated following diagnosis and treatment of an acute febrile tropical illness, with rapid defervescence. Fourteen days after starting antimalarial therapy, while convalescing, he experienced sudden-onset, severe left flank pain, prompting immediate emergency department evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Italian expatriate living in Nigeria for two years. Recently treated for acute tropical infection with antimalarials. No history of abdominal trauma, coagulopathy, hematologic disorder, or splenic disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for sudden acute left flank and left abdominal pain. Negative for recurrent fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, hematuria, or syncope. Medications: completed antimalarial regimen. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs stable on presentation. Abdomen: localized tenderness over left hemiabdomen, but without frank peritonitis, guarding, or rigidity. No palpable masses.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: severe anemia with hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; moderate leukocytosis; platelet count normal. Biochemistry: markedly elevated C-reactive protein (232 mg/L), plasma D-dimer (2,188 ug/L), lactate dehydrogenase (654 IU/L), and creatine kinase (1,255 IU/L). Coagulation assays: within normal limits. Blood cultures: sterile for bacteria and fungi. Peripheral blood smears performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Multidetector computed tomography (CT) of abdomen: diffuse, moderately hyperdense peritoneal fluid consistent with hemoperitoneum, marked splenomegaly with hyperdense stratified subcapsular and perisplenic hematoma, bilateral pleural effusions, and basal atelectasis. Urgent exploratory laparotomy: evacuation of abundant hemorrhagic peritoneal fluid and total splenectomy. Pathology: 850-g ruptured spleen measuring 17x14x8 cm with large capsular laceration, underlying hematoma, diffuse parenchymal hemorrhage, and marked red pulp hyperplasia without malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Spontaneous (non-traumatic) splenic rupture with acute hemoperitoneum complicating convalescent Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
Diagnostic confirmation: Rapid blood assay positive for Plasmodium falciparum antigen; multidetector CT identifying hemoperitoneum and subcapsular splenic hematoma; emergency laparotomy and surgical pathology confirming an 850 g ruptured spleen with red pulp hyperplasia and subcapsular hematoma. Bacterial blood cultures were negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with emergency exploratory laparotomy, evacuation of hemoperitoneum, and total splenectomy. The patient made an uneventful postoperative recovery with stabilization of hemoglobin and was discharged in good condition.
